items.text: Autistic burnout isn't job stress you forgot to manage. Research suggests it's a different physiological state — driven by chronic masking, not overwork. Treating them the same is why 'take a holiday' doesn't help.
items.rationale: Names the core misconception and offers the mechanism without overclaiming. Validates why generic advice fails without prescribing treatment or speaking for all autistic people.
items.sensitivity_flag: The 2026 Ali/Mandy/Happé study is qualitative — it captures lived experience rather than proving distinct physiology via biomarkers. 'Research suggests' hedges this appropriately, but verify the source supports this specific framing before posting.

items.text: Late-diagnosed autistic adults describe a layer of burnout that earlier-diagnosed people don't report in the same way: retrospective grief. Understanding why you suffered doesn't erase it. For many, it deepens it.
items.rationale: Draws directly on the 2026 qualitative study's finding and names the grief dimension with precision. Speaks to an experience rather than universalising across all autistic people.

items.text: The system didn't miss you. It mislabeled you. Neurodivergent wiring that's well-resourced looks like giftedness — until the compensatory system runs out and everyone's confused.
items.rationale: Reframes the 'why didn't anyone catch this?' question by shifting blame from personal failure to structural mislabeling. Punchy without speaking for all neurodivergent people.

items.text: 'You don't seem autistic' is not a compliment. It's a receipt. Proof the disappearing act worked — and post-diagnosis, that praise becomes its own kind of wound.
items.rationale: Names the precise mechanism by which masking compliments become painful after diagnosis. Quotable and specific without being exploitative or pitying.

items.text: There's a specific grief in realizing you've been praised your whole life for how well you could disappear. The compliments were always about the mask.
items.rationale: Softer register than the 'receipt' post — grief-forward rather than reframe-forward. Different entry point to the same insight for people at different stages of processing their diagnosis.

items.text: AuDHD isn't two conditions sitting side by side. It's a constant internal negotiation — needing sameness and novelty about the exact same situation at the exact same moment.
items.rationale: Names the 'half-right in both spaces' experience with enough precision to generate strong recognition. Speaks to an experience rather than defining all AuDHD people.

items.text: Almost all PDA literature is written for parents of children. Autistic adults with a PDA profile are navigating hierarchical workplaces and authority relationships without a map.
items.rationale: States a structural gap plainly. Opens the conversation to adults who may never have seen themselves in the parenting-focused literature, without making clinical claims.

items.text: If a manager's instruction feels disproportionately threatening — not defiance, not immaturity — it may be a nervous system wired to register constraint as danger.
items.rationale: Reframes the PDA workplace experience without requiring a diagnosis label. 'May be' is deliberately tentative. Shifts the story from character flaw to nervous-system difference.
items.sensitivity_flag: Nervous-system language is experiential community framing, not a clinical claim — but 'wired to register constraint as danger' could read as causal-biological to some readers. Verify this framing is defensible from the source before posting.

items.text: Research now names what PDA parents have said privately for years: they feel systematically dismissed by the professionals meant to help them. That's not a personal failing. It's a structural one.
items.rationale: Validates a specific experience with research backing. The pivot from private feeling to structural failure reframes isolation without dwelling in resentment or assigning blame to individuals.

items.text: Low-demand parenting principles — fewer unnecessary demands, genuine choice, connection over compliance — work on yourself too. Not a parenting style. A nervous-system strategy.
items.rationale: Makes the crossover from parenting framework to adult self-management immediately practical and accessible to non-parents. Short enough to be actionable; doesn't prescribe specific behaviors or claim therapeutic effect.

items.text: The collapse — job loss, a new baby, a health crisis — looks like a breakdown from the outside. It's often just the moment the compensatory system finally ran out of fuel.
items.rationale: Names the specific trigger point for late-diagnosis recognition without framing it as a personal failure. 'Finally ran out of fuel' is mechanical and non-pathologizing — describes a system, not a character.

items.text: The post-diagnosis immersion phase has a recognizable shape. What comes after is less mapped. What did integration look like for you — and how did you know you'd arrived?
items.rationale: Opens a forward-looking conversation without pathologizing any phase of the identity arc. Genuine gap in community discourse — invites honest replies from people at different stages without manufactured stakes.
